newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Strikes to cripple S.Korean industry to year end.
newsitem.headline: Strikes to cripple S.Korean industry to year end.

text.p: South Korea on Friday faced a crippling general strike at least until the end of this year, after the nation's biggest union body called out its 1.2 million members in protest at a new labour law.
The Korea Federation of Trade Unions had planned a 24-hour stoppage from 1.00 p.m. (0400 GMT) on Friday, but its chairman said the walkout would now last initially until the year end.
Park In-sang said a decision on whether to further extend the strike would be taken on Monday.
He told a news conference bus services in six cities, including Seoul, would be halted. Subway lines in Seoul operated by federation workers would stop on Monday morning.

But gas, electricity and phone services would not be affected unless the strikes dragged on "and are carried out to extremes". Efforts would be made not to disrupt life for ordinary citizens, Park said.
"We will fight for democracy and the livelihood of the workers," Park said.
"If the strikes are extended into the new year that will basically mean an indefinite strike."

The federation, generally seen as moderate, is the only union umbrella organisation recognised by the government. Its new militancy is an ominous development that raises the stakes in the most serious worker unrest in the nation since the late 1980s.
The outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions, called out its 500,000 members on an indefinite strike on Thursday.
Hospital workers walked out on Friday, leaving only emergency care, as industrial action spread from factories and shipyards to key services.
Nurses and orderlies closed out-patient sections of 14 hospitals, including Seoul National University Hospital, the country's leading medical centre.

The leading employers' group sought to calm workers by promising that controversial provisions of the new law allowing layoffs and flexible working hours would be used only as a last resort by struggling companies.
The law was railroaded through parliament on Thursday.

Layoffs would only occur if firms were in "extreme difficulties" and flexible working hours would not result in a loss in pay, the Korea Employers Federation pledged in a statement. Workers were urged to return to their jobs "because companies are suffering and the economy is not doing well".
The law gives employers the right to replace striking workers. But federation official Ko Song-nam indicated that member companies would not seek to use this provision to break the current strikes.
"If the strikes go on, it is possible that there will be suspensions," he said. "Only in extreme cases will we close factories or use substitute workers".

Several hundred thousand workers from the half million-strong Korea Confederation responded to Thursday's call to down tools, halting production at South Korea's largest car plant, Hyundai Motor, and major shipyards.
Daewoo Group's shipyard was idled on Friday and workers at Daewoo car plants were set to join the stoppages.
Vehicle and ship production in South Korea is now virtually halted. Cars and ships are among the country's top exports.
Seoul subway workers belonging to the outlawed union plan to strike from Saturday, a half day for most workers, threatening transport chaos for tens of thousands of commuters in the capital.
The government declared the strikes illegal, but although it has threatened "stern countermeasures" there was no sign yet of any crackdown on organised labour.

Opposition members of parliament staged an overnight sit-down protest against the government's tactics in ramming through the labour law and another controversial law boosting the powers of the once-notorious domestic spy agency.
They vowed to occupy the chamber until midnight on Saturday.
The bills were passed at a dawn session on Thursday of the National Assembly attended only by ruling New Korea Party members.
